title: Sharknado Probability Risk Analysis
text:
Preface
You are a data scientist for a mid-sized business, in a small group of 3-4 data scientists. You’ve been tasked with creating a report evaluating a scenario for your business. Your colleagues will also be evaluating the same scenario, and your reports will be used in aggregate to determine a consensus (or lack thereof) on the company’s action. The reports will also be used to inform downsizing that is rumored to be coming - you want to ensure your report is better than your peers so that you aren’t as easy to cut.
You may talk to your peers who are assigned the same scenario, but you do not want to collaborate too closely, lest you both become targets of the rumored layoffs.

I’ve scaffolded this report for you to make this process easier - as we talk about different sections of a report in class and read about how to create similar sections, you will practice by writing the equivalent section of your report.
The basic steps for this task are as follows:

Identify the research question from the business question
Identify data set(s) which are (1) publicly available (you don’t have a budget to pay for private data) and (2) relevant to your task

(HW Week 6) Document your data sets in draft-data-doc.qmd

Conduct a statistical analysis to support your answer to your research and business questions

Write a methods section for your business report corresponding to your statistical analysis
(HW Week 9) Draft of results section of business report with relevant graphics/visual aids in draft-results.qmd

Write your report

(HW Week 10) Draft of Intro/Conclusion sections in draft-intro-conclusions.qmd
(HW Week 11) Draft of Executive summary section in draft-exec-summary.qmd

Revise your report

(HW Week 12 – not turned in) Revise your report
(HW Week 13) - Rough draft of report due. Create one or more qmd files for your report (you can overwrite or delete intro.qmd and summary.qmd), include the names of each file (in order) in _quarto.yml. You should use references (edit references.bib and use pandoc citations). Make sure your report compiles and looks reasonable in both html and pdf.
Develop a presentation to go along with your report (Week 13). Create slides for your report using quarto.

Peer revise reports

Peer revise reports
(HW Week 14) - Make edits to your report from comments received from peer review

Final report & presentation due

title: 2  Introduction
text:
Extreme weather events have long piqued public and scientific interest, especially when their consequences can be extremely dangerous for human life. Among these, the concept of a “sharknado,” a tornado capable of lifting sharks from the ocean and throwing them inland, represents an exaggerated but intriguing scenario. While such an event is widely seen as fictional, evaluating a sharknado’s plausibility provides an opportunity to apply probabilistic reasoning within real-world constraints.
This project aims to estimate the probability of a sharknado occurring by breaking up the phenomenon into a sequence of events that need to occur. In the methods section, we outline the sequence of these probabilities. These include the probability of a tornado forming near a coastal region and moving inward, the probability that such a tornado reaches a sufficient intensity to pick up and move a shark, and the assumption that a shark is present at the exact location required. To ensure a conservative upper estimate for this probability, several assumptions are intentionally biased in favor of the event occuring, such as a constant availability of sharks along coastlines and the ability for high magnitude earthquakes to pick them up and transport them inland.








flowchart LR
    A(Tornado forms near coast) --> B(Tornado moves inland)
    B --> C(Tornado strong enough to lift shark)
    C --> D(Shark present at location)
    D --> E((SHARKNADO))








Figure 2.1: Flowchart illustrating the sequence of events leading to a Sharknado.



Using a combination of probabilistic reasoning and simplifying assumptions, the analysis synthesizes these individual components into an overall estimate for the probability of the occurrence of a sharknado. These results provide insight not only into the probability of a sharknado, but also into how compounding rare events together quickly diminishes the overall probability.

title: Appendix B — Methods
text:
A table summarizing the tornado data from the NOAA and their possible values is below:
In the original US tornado data set from the NOAA, many tornadoes have missing ending latitudes and logitudes, specifically they were marked as “0” instead of “NA”. This can’t be right however since the 0 latitude line and the 0 longitude line do not intersect the US anywhere. The red dotted lines below show 0 latitude and and 0 longitude.
As such, these tornadoes in the data set are taken to be rows with missing values. It should be examined whether these tornadoes have some sort of trend relative to the other tornadoes in the data set, so that it can be determined if they can be removed without worry. Specifically, there are two possible concerns: whether tornadoes in a certain area have a significantly higher chance of missing end values, and whether tornadoes of different magnitudes are more likely to have missing end coordinates than others. To examine the first concern, two figures can be created. One of these shows the location of all tornadoes in the data set, and the other shows the location of only the tornadoes that have a missing value for the ending latitude or longitude.
There does not appear to be any trend in the missing end coordinates. The missing end coordinates plot does not appear to have a different trend in location than the plot with all tornadoes. This suggests that our first concern is alleviated.
For the second concern regarding the magnitude, a plot can be created for each magnitude level and examine if there is any difference in the incidence of missing end coordinates depending on the magnitude.
From these plots, it can be seen that none of the magnitudes show a large difference in location on the map. This alleviates the second concern as well, and as such, we can remove these tornadoes without worry about affecting our inference on the probability of a sharknado.
To examine the potential risk of a sharknado, we compute the probability of such an event occurring. From the perspective of any tornado occurring in the USA, this probability can be expressed as the product of several individual probabilities: \[
P(\text{sharknado}) =
P(\text{shark is present}) \times
P(\text{tornado is coastal to inland}) \times
P(\text{tornado is strong enough to lift a shark})
\] Alternatively, if we focus specifically on tornadoes that are coastal-to-inland, the probability of a sharknado occurring conditional on a tornado being coastal to inland can be expressed as:
\[
P(\text{sharknado | tornado is coastal to inland}) =
P(\text{shark is present}) \times
P(\text{tornado is strong enough to lift a shark | tornado is coastal to inland})
\]
The latter case is likely the better answer to our question, as we are worried about the possibility of sharknados occurring when there is a coastal to inland tornado, not when there is a tornado anywhere. As such, the following analysis will focus on the latter case.
To obtain a very conservative upper estimate of this probability, we assume that the probability a shark is present is 100%. In other words, we assume that whenever a coastal to inland tornado occurs, a shark is present near the coast and available to be lifted. While this assumption is not necessarily realistic, it provides a conservative upper bound on the probability of a sharknado. This will strengthen the evidence when the probability of a sharknado is still quite low.
See Figure 2.1 for a flowchart illustrating these necessities.
Change to results here
To start, we must classify each tornado as being coastal to inland, inland to coastal, or neither. This could be done as just coastal to inland or not coastal to inland, but for thoroughness, we included another group for inland to coastal as well to compare.
The threshold used to decide upon “coastal to inland” was if the starting distance of the tornado was within 10000 meters of the closest coast and the ending distance of the tornado was further from the closest coast than the starting distance was. Likewise, tornadoes were classified into the “inland to coastal” group if they were more than 10000 meters from the closest coast and the ending distance of the tornado was closer to the coast than the starting distance.
Coastal to Inland | Inland to Coastal
Change to results here
Now we need to compute the probabilities for each tornado type that we have classified. This can be done quite simply by dividing the number of tornadoes that we have classified to each tornado type by the total number of tornadoes. The results are summarized in the following table:
As shown, there are far fewer coastal-to-inland tornadoes compared with inland-to-coastal and other tornadoes. This relatively small amount reflects the strict requirement that the tornado must start within a short distance of the coast to be classified in this category.
Lastly, we must compute the probability the tornado is strong enough to lift a shark given that the tornado is coastal to inland. Based on Fisheries (2025), we see that great white sharks can be up to 4500 lbs. Based on Quach (n.d.), we see that cars weigh on average 4419 lbs. This suggests that the weight of these great whites is comparable to cars. From Otero Property Adjusting & Appraisals (2025), we see that EF3 tornadoes are “likely to toss cars and trucks,” but EF4 tornadoes are “very likely to toss cars many feet.” This suggests that at least a magnitude 4 tornado would be needed, as for a sharknado to occur, we need the sharks to be picked up and tossed quite far onto land, not just to be picked up and tossed slightly. To compute this probability, we first have to define the number of tornadoes for each combination of magnitude \(m\) and movement type \(t\), call this \(N_{m,t}\). The probability of a tornado having magnitude \(m\) given movement type \(t\) is the number of tornadoes with magnitude \(m\) and movement type \(t\) divided by the total number of tornadoes with movement type \(t\).
\[
P(\text{Magnitude} = m|\text{Movement} = t) = \frac{N_{m,t}}{\sum_{m} N_{m,t}}
\] For our specific probability we are interested in this probability where m = 4 or 5, and t = coastal to inland.
Computing this probability we get: \[
\frac{1 + 0}{417}
\approx 0.2398082\%
\quad
(1 \text{ from magnitude 4},\ 0 \text{ from magnitude 5})
\]
It is important to note that even this very low probability is a conservative upper estimate. We assume that a shark is present along the coast whenever a coastal-to-inland tornado occurs and that a magnitude 4 tornado could lift a shark from the ocean onto land. These assumptions strongly favor the occurrence of a sharknado, since magnitude 4 tornadoes have only been observed lifting cars (objects of similar weight to sharks) several feet off the ground. D Introduction
Extreme weather events have long piqued public and scientific interest, especially when their consequences can be extremely dangerous for human life. Among these, the concept of a “sharknado,” a tornado capable of lifting sharks from the ocean and throwing them inland, represents an exaggerated but intriguing scenario. While such an event is widely seen as fictional, evaluating a sharknado’s plausibility provides an opportunity to apply probabilistic reasoning within real-world constraints.

In the methods section, we outline the sequence of these probabilities. These include the probability of a tornado forming near a coastal region and moving inward, the probability that such a tornado reaches a sufficient intensity to pick up and move a shark, and the assumption that a shark is present at the exact location required. To ensure a conservative upper estimate for this probability, several assumptions are intentionally biased in favor of the event occuring, such as a constant availability of sharks along coastlines and the ability for high magnitude earthquakes to pick them up and transport them inland.

    A(Tornado forms near coast) --> B(Tornado moves inland)
    B --> C(Tornado strong enough to lift shark)
    C --> D(Shark present at location)
    D --> E((SHARKNADO))












Note



Label, caption, cite in the paragraph.


Using a combination of probabilistic reasoning and simplifying assumptions, the analysis synthesizes these individual components into an overall estimate for the probability of the occurrence of a sharknado. These results provide insight not only into the probability of a sharknado, but also into how compounding rare events together quickly diminishes the overall probability.


E Conclusion
The analysis demonstrates that even under highly favorable assumptions, the probability of a sharknado occurring remains extremely low. By breaking down the event into a series of necessary events, each with a very small likelihood, the combined probability becomes effectively zero. Notably, the assumption that sharks are always available along the coastline and that tornadoes of sufficient magnitude can lift them inland represents a significant overestimation, reinforcing that the calculated probability serves as a conservative upper estimate, rather than a realistic expectation.
This extremely low probability is to be expected as we are forcing many rare events to occur simultaneously. When this happens, the overall probability decreases dramatically. This idea extends beyond the concept of sharknadoes and is relevant for other concerns where many rare events need to occur together. In these scenarios, the overall likelihood will drop dramatically as the sharknado probability did.
Future work could build upon this analysis by incorporating more realistic environmental constraints, such as the distribution of shark locations and the physics-based modeling of lifting forces required for moving sharks. Ultimately, while sharnadoes are far from realistic, the analytical approach used in this study shows the power of probabilistic reasoning in exploring even the most unusual problems.

title: Appendix D — Draft: Executive Summary
text:
The purpose of this report is to examine the probability of a “sharknado” by enforcing the real world constraints of such a phenomenon. The primary objective is to estimate the likelihood of a sharknado by sequencing the probability of all the events that must occur together, and evaluating them using avaiable tornado data and reasonable assumptions.
The methodology starts by addressing missing values in the dataset. Specifically, there are many tornadoes in the original data set that have missing values for the ending latitude or longitude. These tornadoes are excluded from the analysis. This is okay to do as the tornadoes with missing values don’t appear to have any bias in their location. The section continues by describing the probabilities that are sequenced together.
These are:

The probability that a shark is present for the tornado to pick up
The probability that a tornado is coastal to inland
The probability that the tornado is strong enough to lift a shark.

A key assumption made is that sharks are always available to be picked up when a coastal to inland tornado occurs. This assumption creates a great overestimate in the probability as it very much favors the occurrence of a sharknado. This ensures that if the resulting probability is still extremely small, then the sharknado risk is essentially nonexistent.
In the results, the probabilities are computed. It is emphasized that the real world constraints for a sharknado to actually happen cause the probability to be very small. This reflects the idea that sharnadoes are simply a product of fiction, and have effectively no risk in real life.
Based on the findings of this analysis, no action needs to be taken to adjust insurance products for the risk of sharknados. The probability of such an event happening is effectively zero, and as a result, any expected claims would also be zero. Time and resources are better allocated towards models accounting for other more likely catastrophic events such as tsunamis, hurricanes, or standard tornadoes.

title: 1  Executive Summary
text:
This report estimates the probability of a “sharknado” by incorporating real-world constraints and combining the probabilities of the events required for such an occurrence. Using available tornado data and reasonable assumptions, the analysis evaluates the likelihood of three key components:

The presence of a shark on the coast
A tornado moving coastal to inland
A tornado is strong enough to lift and move a shark inland

The methodology excludes tornadoes with missing ending coordinates, as these observations show no bias with respect to geographic location or tornado magnitude. The analysis then sequences the relevant probabilities to estimate the overall likelihood. A key assumption is that sharks are always present when a coastal-to-inland tornado occurs, which intentionally overestimates the probability and provides a conservative upper bound.
The results indicate that, even under favorable assumptions, the probability of a sharknado is effectively zero. This supports the conclusion that sharknadoes are purely fictional and pose no real-world risk.






Important



The probability of a sharknado is effectively zero. As such, no adjustments to insurance products are warranted. Resources should instead focus on higher-probability catastrophic events such as hurricanes and standard tornadoes.
